items.question: A network is pretrained on the sentence "Rates rose again in May". Which is one training example it takes from it?

options.text: Input "Rates rose again in", label "May"
Input the whole sentence, label "true"
options.why: Pretraining never labels text true or false. The label is the next token.

options.text: Input "May", label "Rates"
options.why: That runs backwards. The input is the tokens so far; the label is the one after.

options.text: Input a question, label a person's answer
options.why: Questions with written answers are fine-tuning data, not pretraining.

feedback.correct: The tokens so far are the input; the next token is the label.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what is hidden and asked for in pretraining.

explain.text: At every place in the text, the tokens so far are the input. The real next token is the label. "Rates rose again in" followed by "May" is one such example.

items.question: A base model is given "Ingredients: 2 eggs, 100 g flour,". What does it most likely write next?

options.text: More ingredients, such as milk or butter
A reply such as "Sounds like a lovely cake."
options.why: A chatty reply is an assistant's habit. A base model continues the list.

options.text: Nothing, because no question was asked
options.why: A base model needs no question. It continues the text.

options.text: A check that the amounts are correct
options.why: It does not check anything. It writes what usually follows.

feedback.correct: A list of ingredients usually goes on with more ingredients.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A base model continues the text it is given.

explain.text: In text, a list of ingredients usually goes on with more ingredients. A base model writes what usually follows, so it carries on the list.

items.question: Put the three training stages, and what follows them, in order.

lines.text: Pretrain on a huge body of web text
Fine-tune on example chats written by people
Train on people's rankings of pairs of replies

feedback.correct: Web text, example chats, rankings, then use.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each stage starts from the model the stage before made.

byKey.s2: Fine-tuning starts from a base model, so pretraining comes first.
byKey.s3: Raters rank replies an assistant wrote, so fine-tuning comes before the rankings.
byKey.s4: Users meet the chatbot only after all three stages.

explain.text: Pretraining makes a base model, fine-tuning turns it into an assistant, and rankings shape that assistant into the chatbot. Users come last.

items.question: A firm fine-tunes a model on 500 chats in which its agents repeat the firm's slogan. What changes most?

options.text: Its replies start to use the slogan and the agents' style
It learns a great many new facts about the world
options.why: You gave fine-tuning the job of adding facts. A small set of chats mostly changes style and habits.

options.text: Nothing, since 500 chats is too few to change anything
options.why: A few hundred chats are enough to change habits such as a slogan.

options.text: The network grows to fit the new chats
options.why: Fine-tuning trains the same network further; its size does not change.

feedback.correct: Fine-tuning copies the habits in its examples, slogan included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what fine-tuning mostly changes.

explain.text: Fine-tuning copies the habits in its examples. Repeating the slogan is a habit, so the replies pick it up; facts come mostly from pretraining.

rows: What will the pound be worth in euros next March?
Which share will rise most this year?
No one can know that. I can explain how analysts compare shares.

items.question: Tap the example chat that would teach an assistant not to guess.

feedback.correct: Example C admits it cannot know and offers what it can do.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reply that admits it cannot know.

byKey.r0: Example A gives a figure no one could know. Training on it teaches guessing.
byKey.r1: Example B is a fine reply, but its question has an answer. It teaches nothing about doubt.

explain.text: Example C pairs an unknowable question with an honest reply. Fine-tuning copies that habit, so the assistant learns to say when it cannot know.

items.question: Raters at a firm prefer the longer of two replies most of the time. What happens to the chatbot trained on their rankings?

options.text: Its replies tend to get longer, useful or not
Its replies get better in every way
options.why: They get longer. Longer is not the same as better.

options.text: Its replies become more truthful
Nothing changes, since raters disagree
options.why: Here most raters agree on length, so it moves that way.

feedback.correct: The model moves towards what the rankings reward: here, length.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The model follows the rankings.

explain.text: Training from feedback makes the preferred kind of reply more likely. These raters prefer length, so replies grow longer whether or not that helps.

items.question: A chatbot gives a firm's founding year and adds "I am sure of this". What does the added sentence tell you?

options.text: Nothing about whether the year is right
That the year is right, since it is sure
options.why: "I am sure" is likely text, written the same way as the year.

options.text: That it looked the year up
options.why: There is no list of facts to look up. It predicted the year.

options.text: That the year is probably wrong
options.why: Sure-sounding answers are often right too. The words tell you nothing either way.

feedback.correct: Nothing. The phrase is likely text, not a check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the phrase was written.

explain.text: "I am sure of this" is written the same way as the year: as likely text. A right year and a wrong one can both come with it.

items.question: Use the ai-basics text "the cat sat on the mat . the cat ate the jam . the dog sat on the cat ." What is the chance its table writes "the dog sat on the cat sat on the mat ." after "the"? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 5 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write down the chance of every pair, then multiply.

byKey.missed-third: You left out "sat" after "cat", which has chance $\tfrac13$: cat is followed by sat, ate and ".".
byKey.two-sixths: You kept only the two $\tfrac16$ pairs. "cat" after "the" ($\tfrac12$) and "sat" after "cat" ($\tfrac13$) count too.

explain.text: Four pairs have chance below 1. They are dog after the ($\tfrac16$), cat after the ($\tfrac12$), sat after cat ($\tfrac13$) and mat after the ($\tfrac16$). Their product is $\tfrac{1}{216}$, about 0.00463, for a sentence the text never says.

lines: You: Tell me about saving into a pension.
Chatbot: A pension is a way to save for retirement.
Chatbot: Tax relief for most savers is 20%.
Chatbot: A 2019 report by the Pension Review Office found 1 in 3 savers stop early.
Chatbot: Starting early usually helps, because savings have longer to grow.
params.title: An invented example

items.question: Tap the lines that state a specific claim you must check before using.

feedback.correct: The rate and the report are specific claims; check both.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a specific number or a named source.

byKey.l2: That a pension is a way to save for retirement is general and widely known.
byKey.l5: That starting early usually helps is a general remark, not a specific claim.
byKey.l1: That is your own question, not a claim.

explain.text: A specific rate and a named report can each be invented and read the same as real ones. General, widely known remarks carry little risk. Check the specific claims first.

items.question: Why can a fluent chatbot state a false fact?

options.text: It writes likely text, and likely is not the same as true
It tells lies on purpose to mislead people
options.why: It has no aim to mislead. Likely text can be false all by itself.

options.text: It only happens when the chatbot is broken
options.why: It happens in a chatbot working as trained.

options.text: It cannot happen once a chatbot is well trained
options.why: Better training can make it rarer. It does not make every likely sentence true.

feedback.correct: Likely text can be false, and nothing checks it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a model is trained to write.

explain.text: A model writes likely text, and a likely sentence need not be true. Joining likely pieces can give a fluent statement nothing supports.
